paragraphs: 360-MLC adapts a pretrained room-layout predictor to a new domain using unlabeled panoramic images. Its central assumption is geometric: predictions made from different camera positions in the same room should describe a consistent layout. Agreement across views therefore provides a learning signal when annotated room boundaries are unavailable.

The method projects predicted boundaries from several views into shared three-dimensional coordinates, then projects them back into spherical image coordinates. It constructs a probability function from these predictions and samples pseudo-labels for training. Where the projected boundaries disagree, their variance serves as an uncertainty estimate, reducing the influence of less confident pseudo-labels.

The paper also uses entropy across layout estimates to measure geometric consistency. This gives a way to tune hyperparameters and select models without ground-truth annotations. Experiments adapting from three public source datasets to a newly labeled dataset of multiple views per scene report favorable performance against leading methods. The contribution connects adaptation and model selection through the same cross-view consistency principle.
neurips-2022-360-mlc-multi-view-layout-c.tldr: 360-MLC uses agreement across panoramic views to adapt room-layout models and select hyperparameters without ground-truth annotations.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated minimax optimization, where agents jointly optimize competing minimization and maximization objectives while keeping local objective functions private. Agents can compute locally and communicate with a central server. The challenge is to reduce communication while retaining a reliable path to an accurate global solution.

The authors first analyze Local Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent under the idealized condition of noiseless gradients. They show that constant step sizes generally cannot guarantee exact convergence, helping explain why shrinking step sizes and slower convergence arise. Their proposed method, FedGDA-GT, adds gradient tracking to federated gradient descent ascent.

For local objectives that are Lipschitz smooth and strongly convex–strongly concave, FedGDA-GT achieves linear convergence with a constant step size. Reaching an epsilon-accurate solution requires communication rounds logarithmic in inverse accuracy, matching the stated centralized iteration complexity. The paper also gives generalization bounds using Rademacher complexity and reports numerical improvements over Local SGDA. Its fast convergence guarantee depends on the specified objective assumptions.
neurips-2022-a-communication-efficient-a.tldr: FedGDA-GT uses gradient tracking to obtain fast, communication-efficient federated minimax optimization under smoothness and strong convexity–concavity assumptions.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer the rewards behind an expert’s behavior. Many approaches assume that environment dynamics are known or that a generative model can supply samples. AceIRL addresses the more restrictive access setting in which the learner must gather information through sequential interaction with an unknown environment and expert policy.

AceIRL uses observations already collected to build confidence intervals describing plausible reward functions. These intervals guide exploration toward regions expected to provide useful information. Exploration thus supports two connected goals: learning the expert’s reward function and identifying a good policy, rather than collecting experience without regard to current uncertainty.

The paper provides sample-complexity guarantees without requiring a generative environment model. Its worst-case bound matches that of active inverse reinforcement learning with such a model. A further problem-dependent bound links the required samples to the problem’s suboptimality gap. Simulation results show significant improvements over more naive exploration strategies, supporting the value of directing interaction toward informative parts of the environment.
neurips-2022-active-exploration-for-inve.tldr: AceIRL actively gathers informative sequential experience to learn expert rewards, with sample-complexity guarantees that do not require a generative environment model.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different descriptions of the same data to find groups. Anchor graph methods make this scalable by representing relationships through selected representative anchors instead of computing every pairwise similarity. This paper identifies a problem in combining those graphs: corresponding columns can refer to different anchors across views.

Combining unaligned columns can mix unrelated relationships and harm clustering. Matching anchors is difficult because different views may use feature spaces with different dimensions. The proposed FMVACC framework uses both feature information and graph structure to establish anchor correspondences. Only after this alignment does it fuse the graphs column by column.

The authors establish theoretical connections to existing late-fusion and partially view-aligned clustering approaches, showing how their framework relates to broader multi-view methods. Experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. Applying the alignment module to existing anchor graph methods also produces significant performance improvements. These findings support anchor correspondence as an important part of graph fusion, rather than an incidental implementation detail.
neurips-2022-align-then-fusion-generaliz.tldr: FMVACC improves multi-view clustering by matching representative anchors across views before combining their graphs.

paragraphs: A spiking neuron fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold. In biological neurons, that threshold can change to help maintain a stable overall firing rate, a property called homeostasis. This paper brings that regulatory idea into spiking neural networks through a bioinspired dynamic energy-temporal threshold scheme, BDETT.

BDETT follows two biological observations. The threshold is positively related to average membrane potential and negatively related to the preceding rate of depolarization. In plain terms, the firing threshold responds both to the neuron’s average internal state and to how quickly that state was rising. This makes the threshold part of the neuron’s changing behavior rather than a fixed setting.

The authors evaluate BDETT on robot obstacle avoidance and continuous control. Tests include normal operation and degraded conditions involving noisy observations, noisy weights, and changing environments. BDETT significantly outperforms static and heuristic threshold approaches in every tested condition. The results also support its ability to provide homeostasis in these tasks, connecting biologically motivated firing regulation with practical control performance.
neurips-2022-biologically-inspired-dynam.tldr: BDETT adapts spiking thresholds using biological principles, improving control performance and firing-rate stability in the tested conditions.

paragraphs: Training a large model across distributed machines requires exchanging information, but the number of model parameters may greatly exceed the number of training examples. This paper asks how many communication bits are fundamentally needed to reach zero or nearly zero training loss in such overparameterized problems.

For a class of models with far more parameters D than data samples N, the authors establish a lower bound proportional to N. This lower bound does not depend on D. It identifies a fundamental communication requirement tied to the amount of training data, providing a target for algorithms that avoid costs scaling with every model parameter.

The paper then develops algorithms for linear regression and certain multilayer neural networks containing one wide layer. These methods combine linear compression with adaptive quantization and achieve communication complexity independent of parameter dimension, sometimes approaching the lower bound. The results establish that dimension-independent communication is attainable for the specified models. They do not assert the same algorithmic guarantee for every overparameterized architecture.
neurips-2022-distributed-optimization-fo.tldr: For specified overparameterized models, compression and adaptive quantization enable distributed training with communication costs independent of parameter count.

paragraphs: Dynamic graph models learn from both changing connections and changing node features. A pattern that predicts labels during training can become unreliable when those relationships shift. This paper addresses that problem by seeking spatio-temporal patterns whose predictive usefulness remains stable across changes in the data distribution.

The proposed DIDA model first uses disentangled spatio-temporal attention to capture stable and variable patterns separately. It then samples and recombines variable patterns across neighborhoods and time points, creating multiple intervened distributions. These interventions are designed to remove the misleading influence of patterns whose association with the prediction target can change.

An invariance regularizer penalizes variation in predictions across those intervened distributions. This encourages the model to rely on the stable patterns it has identified. Experiments on three real-world datasets and one synthetic dataset show better performance than leading baselines under distribution shifts. The approach matters because it treats robustness as a training objective involving both graph structure and time, rather than relying only on predictive fit to the observed distribution.
neurips-2022-dynamic-graph-neural-networ.tldr: DIDA separates stable and variable graph patterns and trains predictions to remain consistent when variable patterns are rearranged.

paragraphs: This paper studies sampling from a Gibbs distribution on a Riemannian manifold, a space whose geometry need not be flat. Its geometric Langevin algorithm uses exponential maps to take steps along random Gaussian directions. The goal is to understand how efficiently these discrete updates approach the desired probability distribution.

The central analysis bounds the error introduced by discretizing the continuous geometric process. Assuming a Lipschitz gradient for the energy function and bounded sectional curvature, the error has the same step-size dependence as its Euclidean counterpart. Combining this result with a contraction guarantee gives an iteration bound proportional to inverse squared accuracy, up to logarithmic factors, measured in Wasserstein distance.

The resulting complexity matches the stated Euclidean Langevin rate while allowing nonconvex energy functions and manifolds with negative Ricci curvature. The authors also analyze stochastic-gradient updates. That extension reaches the same accuracy dependence under additional assumptions on curvature derivatives and a curvature-dimension condition for the target distribution. The contribution therefore extends familiar sampling guarantees to broader geometric settings while specifying the regularity conditions needed.
neurips-2022-efficient-sampling-on-riema.tldr: Geometric Langevin sampling matches Euclidean accuracy-dependent iteration rates under stated regularity and contraction conditions.

paragraphs: When useful rewards arrive rarely, a reinforcement learning agent receives little guidance about which behavior to develop. Reward shaping supplies additional learning signals to accelerate training. The paper argues that existing formulations can require outside domain knowledge or fail when the original reward signal is extremely sparse.

Exploration-Guided Reward Shaping, or ExploRS, combines a learned intrinsic reward function with exploration bonuses. The intrinsic reward is learned to improve the agent’s utility under the environment’s extrinsic rewards. This connects the additional training signal to the original task objective while retaining incentives to explore. The framework operates in a fully self-supervised manner.

The authors theoretically demonstrate the usefulness of this construction for a special family of Markov decision processes. Experiments in several environments with sparse or noisy rewards also demonstrate its effectiveness. Together, these results support the idea that exploration bonuses and learned reward shaping can complement each other. The theoretical result is specific to the analyzed family, while the broader practical evidence comes from the reported environments.
neurips-2022-exploration-guided-reward-s.tldr: ExploRS combines learned intrinsic rewards with exploration bonuses to accelerate learning from sparse or noisy task rewards.

paragraphs: Some powerful graph learning methods repeatedly run a graph neural network on extracted subgraphs with customized node labels. Those extra computations help capture structure that plain graph neural networks miss, but they are costly. Geodesic GNN seeks richer structural representations using only one graph neural network run and no customized labeling.

Its key source of context is the shortest paths between two nodes. The model combines embeddings of nodes along those paths into geodesic representations. These representations describe relationships conditioned on the node pair, adding structural context to the embeddings produced by the initial network pass.

Using this context, the framework produces representations for nodes, links, and entire graphs. The authors theoretically prove greater expressive power than plain graph neural networks. Experiments across graph learning tasks show highly competitive performance against leading models while using significantly less time. The findings support shortest-path context as a way to enrich graph representations without the repeated network evaluations used by the subgraph approaches discussed in the paper.
neurips-2022-geodesic-graph-neural-netwo.tldr: Geodesic GNN adds shortest-path context to a single network pass, yielding richer graph representations with substantially lower reported runtime.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks and graph kernels offer different ways to learn from connected data. Combining them promises expressive representations together with the trainability of kernel methods, but the resulting computation can be expensive. This paper also identifies loss of graph structure in straightforward convolution methods as a concern for such models.

GraphQNTK introduces a quantum algorithm that approximately estimates the neural tangent kernel of an underlying graph neural network. The approach uses quantum parallelism with the aim of improving computational efficiency. A multi-head quantum attention mechanism incorporates semantic similarities between nodes, helping the model account for information beyond a straightforward convolutional treatment of the graph.

The authors report competitive results on several graph classification benchmarks and provide theoretical analysis supporting the quantum algorithm’s advantages. These are complementary claims: the experiments address predictive performance, while the theory addresses the proposed algorithm. The contribution is a quantum approach to constructing a graph-learning kernel that considers both structural information and computational cost.
neurips-2022-graphqntk-quantum-neural-ta.tldr: GraphQNTK uses a quantum algorithm and quantum attention to approximate a graph neural tangent kernel with competitive classification performance.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine information from neighboring nodes and often combine all node representations into a whole-graph representation. Common pooling choices include sums, averages, and maxima. This paper focuses on what those simple summaries miss: higher-order nonlinear interactions among nodes, where combinations of node information matter together.

The proposed Tensorized Graph Neural Network, tGNN, models those interactions using tensor decomposition. Specifically, symmetric CP decomposition provides an efficient parameterization of permutation-invariant multilinear maps. Permutation invariance means that the result does not depend on the order in which nodes are presented, preserving an essential property of graph representations while allowing richer interactions.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical analyses supporting tGNN’s advantages over competitive baselines on node and graph classification. They highlight strong results on two OGB node classification datasets and one OGB graph classification dataset. The central contribution is therefore a more expressive aggregation mechanism: it changes how node information is combined, using tensor structure to make higher-order modeling computationally manageable.
neurips-2022-high-order-pooling-for-grap.tldr: tGNN uses tensor decomposition to efficiently model higher-order node interactions while preserving invariance to node ordering.

paragraphs: Outcome-conditioned imitation learning turns an agent’s own experience into training examples. Each experience is labeled with the outcome it actually achieved, and the agent learns to imitate behavior associated with those labels. This is appealing because it connects reinforcement learning to supervised learning through a simple training procedure.

The paper asks whether that procedure serves the standard reinforcement learning objective of maximizing reward. Its main negative result is that existing outcome-conditioned imitation methods do not necessarily improve the policy. Successfully fitting relabeled experience therefore does not, by itself, establish that the resulting behavior earns higher rewards. This challenges a guarantee one might otherwise infer from the method’s intuitive appeal.

The authors then show that a simple modification yields a method with a policy-improvement guarantee. Their purpose is to clarify how a variant of outcome-conditioned imitation can maximize rewards, rather than introduce an entirely new learning paradigm. The distinction matters: the result identifies a gap in existing methods and shows that the overall imitation-based strategy can be repaired.
neurips-2022-imitating-past-successes-ca.tldr: Existing outcome-conditioned imitation need not improve a policy, but the paper shows that a simple modification restores a policy-improvement guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper studies differential privacy for adaptive streams, where later computations can depend on earlier results. Its focus is the matrix mechanism and how to instantiate it optimally in that setting. The motivation comes from machine learning applications in which privacy-preserving computations occur throughout an evolving training process.

The authors establish theoretical results showing how matrix factorizations apply to adaptive streaming. They also introduce a parameter-free fixed-point algorithm for finding optimal factorizations. This supplies both a foundation for using the mechanism in an adaptive setting and a computational procedure for choosing its factorization, connecting the privacy framework to an implementable optimization method.

The framework is instantiated for concrete matrices that arise in machine learning. The resulting mechanisms are then used to train models with user-level differential privacy, and the authors report significant improvements on a federated learning problem. The stated empirical finding concerns that application. The broader contribution is a principled method for computing optimal private linear mechanisms and applying them within adaptive learning.
neurips-2022-improved-differential-priva.tldr: The paper develops optimal matrix mechanisms for adaptive streams and applies them to improve user-level private federated learning.

paragraphs: Worst-case reinforcement learning guarantees describe how difficult the hardest problem can be, but they can obscure substantial differences between individual tasks. This paper studies instance-dependent sample complexity with linear function approximation: how much experience is needed to identify a near-optimal policy for the particular problem being solved.

The proposed PEDEL algorithm uses online experiment design to allocate its exploration budget. It focuses on directions that are most relevant to identifying a near-optimal policy. The resulting complexity measure responds to the structure of the individual instance, aiming to capture opportunities that a worst-case analysis alone does not reveal.

An explicit example shows provable gains over algorithms that are both low-regret and minimax-optimal. In that example, those algorithms cannot achieve the instance-optimal rate. This illustrates that good worst-case or regret guarantees need not imply the best sample efficiency for policy identification on a specific problem. The paper’s contribution is both the finer complexity guarantee and the exploration procedure that makes such targeted learning possible.
neurips-2022-instance-dependent-near-opt.tldr: PEDEL targets exploration toward policy-relevant directions to obtain sample-complexity guarantees tailored to individual linear reinforcement learning problems.

paragraphs: Neural networks learning continuously from new data can lose knowledge acquired earlier, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. This paper introduces the Sequential Neural Coding Network to make learning from data streams more resistant to that loss. Its learning mechanism is based on predictive coding rather than conventional error backpropagation.

The architecture adapts its connections through biologically plausible learning, while a second neural system learns to direct and control the main network. The authors relate this division of responsibilities to a cortex-like structure under task-executive control resembling aspects of the basal ganglia. Local learning and lateral competition are among the biological mechanisms motivating the design.

Experiments on standard benchmarks, including SplitMNIST and Split Fashion MNIST, and custom benchmarks show significantly less forgetting than standard neural models. The system also outperforms multiple prior methods, including approaches that retain data for rehearsal, despite training in a streaming fashion. These findings support biological mechanisms as a productive direction for lifelong learning; the reported result is reduced forgetting, rather than a universal guarantee that forgetting disappears.
neurips-2022-lifelong-neural-predictive-.tldr: A predictive-coding architecture with learned neural control reduces catastrophic forgetting in streaming-learning experiments without using backpropagation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much information in a natural visual scene is needed to explain retinal neural responses. It builds a joint model of visual stimuli and neuronal activity using the information bottleneck framework. The model compresses input into a few latent variables chosen for their usefulness in predicting responses.

A Gaussian process prior accounts for correlations among samples from published experiments on isolated retinas. The resulting IB-GP model predicts spike responses competitively with leading feedforward convolutional networks. It is also used in an iterative closed-loop procedure to construct simpler inputs that elicit responses like those associated with the original stimuli.

The authors report that reconstructed stimuli support robust spike prediction across models, and that the latent representations capture dynamics of both stimuli and retinal ganglion cell responses. The reduced stimuli contain Gabor-like local high-frequency patterns, on- and off-center Gaussian patterns, or mixtures. These findings suggest that a compact joint representation can expose response-relevant visual structure and could help explain computations in the early visual system.
neurips-2022-natural-image-synthesis-for.tldr: An information-bottleneck model compresses natural visual stimuli into response-relevant representations and generates simpler stimuli associated with similar retinal responses.

paragraphs: Cross-silo federated learning involves a limited number of participating organizations, each holding data about many people. This paper argues that protecting an entire client as a single unit is less suitable here than protecting examples within each silo. It studies sample-level differential privacy with privacy targets chosen separately by each silo.

Within that setting, the authors revisit personalization through mean-regularized multi-task learning, or MR-MTL. This framework supports silo-specific learning while encouraging models to stay close to a shared mean. It offers a way to balance differences between silos against the benefits of learning together under privacy-induced noise.

The paper finds that stronger privacy requirements can increase the incentive to collaborate, because greater federation helps mitigate differential privacy noise. MR-MTL provides consistent improvements over standard baselines in the reported study. An accompanying theoretical analysis addresses mean estimation and clarifies the interaction between privacy and data heterogeneity. The contribution establishes a practical baseline while showing that privacy requirements can change how much personalization and sharing are useful.
neurips-2022-on-privacy-and-personalizat.tldr: With silo-specific sample privacy, mean-regularized personalization provides a strong baseline and shows why stronger privacy can favor greater collaboration.

paragraphs: Full waveform inversion reconstructs underground velocity maps from seismic measurements. As data-driven approaches become more prominent, researchers need shared datasets for comparing methods across different geological settings. OpenFWI supplies a large benchmark collection intended to make that research more varied, rigorous, and reproducible.

The collection contains twelve synthesized datasets totaling 2.1 terabytes, with individual dataset sizes ranging from 2,000 to 67,000 samples. It includes settings involving interfaces, faults, and carbon dioxide reservoirs, along with different subsurface structures such as flat and curved formations. A dataset for three-dimensional inversion extends the collection beyond the other included settings.

The authors benchmark four deep learning methods spanning supervised and unsupervised learning. They also conduct studies involving physics-driven methods, complexity, generalization, and uncertainty quantification. Those investigations provide insight into dataset and method behavior while exposing current limitations. OpenFWI’s contribution is therefore both a shared data resource and an initial comparative evaluation, giving future work a common basis for examining more than performance on a single geological configuration.
neurips-2022-openfwi-large-scale-multi-s.tldr: OpenFWI provides twelve diverse seismic inversion datasets and accompanying benchmarks to support reproducible comparisons across geological settings.

paragraphs: Embodied AI agents learn to navigate and act within environments, making the availability of varied training worlds important. ProcTHOR is a procedural generation framework for creating diverse, interactive, customizable virtual environments. It supports generating arbitrarily large datasets for training and evaluating navigation, interaction, and manipulation.

The authors demonstrate the framework using 10,000 generated houses and a simple neural model. Models trained with RGB images, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve reported state-of-the-art results across six embodied AI benchmarks. These benchmarks cover navigation, rearrangement, and arm manipulation, showing the usefulness of generated environments across several kinds of action.

The paper also evaluates transfer without fine-tuning on the downstream benchmark. Pretraining on ProcTHOR produces strong zero-shot results, often exceeding earlier leading systems that used downstream training data. The findings support procedural environment generation as a route to scalable embodied learning. In particular, the transfer results suggest that experience across many generated houses can be useful beyond the environments used during pretraining.
neurips-2022-procthor-large-scale-embodi.tldr: ProcTHOR generates diverse interactive houses at scale, enabling strong embodied-agent performance and zero-shot transfer across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: SCINet is a neural architecture for forecasting time series with complex temporal behavior. It starts from the observation that splitting a series into two downsampled subsequences largely preserves its temporal relationships. This makes the subsequences useful sources of information rather than merely reduced versions that discard the original structure.

The architecture recursively downsamples, applies convolutions, and allows the resulting representations to interact. At each layer, multiple convolutional filters extract different temporal features from the subsequences or their features. Repeating this process produces information at multiple resolutions, which the model combines to represent the dynamics of the series.

The paper reports significant forecasting accuracy improvements over existing convolutional models and Transformer-based approaches across several real-world datasets. These results support the usefulness of combining features from multiple temporal resolutions with interaction between subsequences. The architectural contribution is the coordinated downsample–convolve–interact process: it uses the persistence of temporal relationships after downsampling as a basis for learning richer forecasting representations.
neurips-2022-scinet-time-series-modeling.tldr: SCINet combines convolution and interaction across recursively downsampled time series to improve forecasting on the evaluated real-world datasets.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, a shared reward can make individual contributions difficult to interpret. Value factorization breaks a joint value into agent-level quantities, but the paper argues that its underlying meaning needs stronger theoretical grounding. It uses Shapley value theory to build an interpretable framework for that decomposition.

The authors generalize the Shapley value to Markov convex games, calling the result the Markov Shapley value. Through an equivalence with global reward games, they use this quantity for value factorization. They derive a Shapley-Bellman optimality equation whose optimal values correspond to an optimal joint deterministic policy, and prove that a proposed operator solves that equation.

Stochastic approximation and further transformations turn this framework into Shapley Q-learning, or SHAQ. Its implementation is guided by the theoretical properties of the value and operator. Experiments report superior performance on all tested tasks and interpretations consistent with the analysis. The paper thus links an agent-level allocation of joint value to both a learning algorithm and an explanation of what its factorized values represent.
neurips-2022-shaq-incorporating-shapley-.tldr: SHAQ derives interpretable multi-agent value factorization and Q-learning from a Markov extension of Shapley value theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a linear subspace shared by different users’ mean vectors. Each observed sample is a user’s mean plus independent, mean-zero noise. Motivated by federated learning, the setting allows users to contribute different numbers of samples and to have different amounts and shapes of noise.

With only one sample per user, recovery is information-theoretically impossible when noise covariance can be nonspherical, absent further restrictions. The authors instead use at least two samples from each user. This enables an efficiently computable estimator that handles both direction-dependent noise and differences in noise across users without the restrictive assumptions discussed for earlier work.

The estimator’s error upper bound matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to a constant factor. That lower bound holds even for spherical Gaussian noise, implying that irregular noise adds no extra estimation penalty beyond a constant factor in the stated bounds. The paper also supplies results for a related linear regression setting. Its key message is that repeated observations per user can overcome an identifiability obstacle created by irregular noise.
neurips-2022-subspace-recovery-from-hete.tldr: Using at least two samples per user enables efficient shared-subspace recovery under irregular noise with error bounds optimal up to a constant factor.

paragraphs: Generative flow networks learn to construct objects, such as graphs or strings, through sequences of actions. Their goal is to sample according to a target density whose normalization need not be known. Multiple action sequences may produce the same final object, making learning about the whole construction process important.

The paper identifies inefficient credit propagation in earlier flow-matching and detailed-balance objectives, especially over long action sequences. It proposes trajectory balance as an alternative learning objective. By formulating the learning requirement around trajectories, the method addresses how information about completed outcomes reaches the decisions that produced them.

The authors prove that any global minimizer of the trajectory-balance objective can define a policy that samples exactly from the target distribution. That is a statement about global minimizers, rather than a guarantee for every training run. Experiments in four domains show benefits for convergence, sample diversity, and robustness to long sequences and large action spaces. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support trajectory balance as a more effective training objective for sequential generation.
neurips-2022-trajectory-balance-improved.tldr: Trajectory balance improves GFlowNet credit assignment and has a global-minimum guarantee that can yield exact target-distribution sampling.

paragraphs: End-to-end driving methods often either predict a trajectory for a controller to follow or directly predict vehicle controls. This paper combines those two approaches in a single architecture, aiming to use their complementary strengths. One branch plans future motion, while the other predicts control actions.

The control branch uses a multi-step prediction scheme to reason about the relationship between current actions and future states. At each time step, it receives corresponding guidance from the trajectory branch. The outputs of the two branches are then fused, so the architecture connects planning and direct control both during prediction and when producing the final output.

Evaluation takes place in challenging closed-loop urban driving scenarios in the CARLA simulator. Using only a monocular camera, the approach achieves the reported first-place position on the official CARLA leaderboard, outperforming more complex candidates by a large margin. The result supports the value of integrating trajectory guidance with direct control in the tested simulation setting, where actions influence the subsequent states the system encounters.
neurips-2022-trajectory-guided-control-p.tldr: A two-branch driving model combines trajectory guidance with multi-step direct control and achieves leading reported CARLA performance using one camera.
